My newsletter and podcast wouldn’t exist if I hadn’t taken a sabbatical.

Seven years into my time at Airbnb, I took a three-month break. It was the first time I’d taken more than two weeks off in my more than 15-year career. I spent those months tinkering, reading, and traveling—and even snuck in a 10-day silent meditation retreat. 

At the end of it, I realized my heart wasn’t in the work anymore and that it was time for something new. So I left my job without much of a plan and spent the next six months exploring. Those six months turned into a year, that year turned into my newsletter, and the rest is history.

Looking back, I can say those were among the three most important months of my life, because they led me to what I do now—the most interesting, fulfilling, and impactful work I can ever imagine.

Life makes it hard to get off the default path and back onto a road of your own design. Sometimes that looks like leaving your job, like I did. Other times, it means reconnecting to why you’re doing the work you’re already doing. Either way, in my experience and that of many friends, significant time away from your day-to-day is necessary for the mental, physical, or emotional shift that will reveal what’s next. What you need is what today’s newsletter guest author @djdidonna calls “Big Time Off.”

DJ is the founder of The Sabbatical Project, and today DJ’s book Big Time Off comes out! It’s a deeply researched, beautifully written book on the value of taking time off, with tangible advice, real-world case studies, and practical considerations for anyone who wants to shake things up.

In today's newsletter, DJ shares some excerpts from his book to help you start thinking about what a sabbatical might look like for you now or down the road.

I’ve always wished there were a guide to help me think through this decision and make the most of this precious time off. We finally have one.

Enjoy: https://t.co/QxSro4izSV

How do I use ChatGPT Voice with Codex? 
- I have it running on the side, so I can ramble random exploration that I want to run as a new thread.
- I ask what is running right now, that is the progress on task A and B.
- Any random new ideas I can challenge myself instantly, refine a prompt, ask for Codex to send the refined prompt on my behalf to any task.
- I ask what open PR are assigned to me for review, what they do, what their end user behaviour is.
- I ask what the status on my own open PR, any review feedbacks, do I need to take any actions? 
- I can ask the voice to split a big chunk of work for me. Plan a new feature, refine and validate the plan, ask for Codex to spawn multiple parallel tasks and worktrees so the work can be done at the same time. 
- Ask to generate concept arts for a game I want to build. Just rambling some ideas I have and asking to use imagegen to generate me the game concepts in various states.
- Not sure about some wording? I ask for what is the right word, what will be the most effective way to put my intent into motion.

rt_of.author: Pragmatic_Eng
rt_of.text:
Why did spec-driven development never take off - the workflow tools like Amazon’s Kiro or GitHub Workspaces encouraged? @dexhorthy, founder of HumanLayer:

“These projects have a really interesting idea: you maintain a set of specifications for your software, and then you maintain the code itself, and the dream is the coding part is just compiling specs into code.

But that part never really materialized. I’m on a GitHub issue in spec kit that’s been open for a year, and every couple of weeks I get a new email on the thread of people complaining about the same problem:

I edit my specs and then I edit the code, and the code drifts from the specs. How do I keep the specs up to date as the code is changing?

You now have two sources of truth, and it stops being useful. That’s why with RPI (Research, Plan, Implement), the docs are tactical execution docs -  I do the research, the plan, the implementation, and I throw the docs out. 

The next time I need research I just do it from scratch, because tokens are cheap and my time is expensive.”

// Agentic Context Management //

Great read for the weekend.

(bookmark it)

Production agents fail less on reasoning and more on what sits in their context. Conversation history, big prompts, huge tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs pile up every turn.

The common response is storage and retrieval, a place to stash memories and look them up. New research argues that framing is too narrow and names a fuller discipline, Agentic Context Management.

It decomposes into five primitives, architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting with consolidation.

Naive accumulation grows token cost with the square of conversation length. Crude summarization buys linear cost but hits an accuracy cliff. Only compaction validated against fidelity gets you linear cost without losing what matters.

A reference implementation reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo.

Why does it matter?

Context management is becoming a first-class production concern that operates across an entire organization. The five primitives give you a structured way to reason about where your token budget goes.

Paper: https://t.co/mKdZNVnqLv

Learn to build effective AI agents in our academy: https://t.co/1e8RZKs4uX

items.text:
Here's how we can progressively build from supervised training to RL, agentic RL, and finally a unified RL + world modeling objective…

Each of the steps mentioned above is outlined in greater detail below. An implementation of each step in PyTorch is provided in the attached images for reference.

Supervised training teaches an LLM to predict the next token in a sequence using a cross entropy loss. The supervision comes directly from the training data (i.e., the ground truth next token is already present in every example). During training, we maximize the likelihood of these ground-truth tokens. This same objective is used for both pretraining and supervised finetuning (SFT).

Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an LLM on its own generations (i.e., on-policy learning) instead of ground-truth / supervised text. The model first samples completions, receives a reward for each rollout (from a verifier or reward model), and then updates its policy to increase the probability of high-reward outputs using some policy gradient algorithm. More specifically, Policy gradient algorithms—like PPO or GRPO—implement this by weighting each generated token according to its advantage, encouraging behaviors that lead to better outcomes.

Agentic RL extends this same idea from single-step LLMs to multi-step agents. Rather than producing output in a single step, the model repeatedly generates actions, invokes tools, and receives observations from its environment over many interaction steps (i.e., within an agentic loop). The learning objective of agentic RL remains largely unchanged relative to standard RL: we simply compute the RL loss over the agent-generated action tokens while masking out environment observations (or other tokens that are not generated by the LLM). Besides such action masking, the implementation remains the same relative to standard RL.

Agentic world modeling combines supervised learning and (agentic) RL into a single objective. LLM-generated action tokens are optimized with an advantage-weighted RL loss, while observation tokens receive a constant positive weight that reduces to supervised next-token prediction. This hybrid objective simultaneously teaches the model what actions to take and how its environment responds, allowing the agent to improve both decision making and its internal simulation of the world. This is a hybrid agent and world model!
